title: How do you implement multi-tenancy in an API Gateway?
shortTitle: How to implement multi-tenancy in an API Gateway

s1_definition.profdef: Multi-tenancy is serving many independent customers, called tenants, from one shared platform while keeping each tenant's data, configuration, and resource usage strictly isolated. At the gateway, multi-tenancy is implemented by identifying the tenant on every request, from a subdomain, a path prefix, a header, or a claim in the JWT; attaching that tenant identity to the request context and propagating it downstream; and then applying per-tenant policy such as routing, rate limits, quotas, and data isolation. The gateway becomes the authoritative place where every request is stamped with a verified tenant so no tenant can ever see or affect another.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India runs a shared platform that several partner banks use, each a separate tenant. It is like one big office building where each partner bank rents its own floor. The security desk at the entrance, the gateway, looks at each visitor's pass to see which bank they belong to, stamps their file with that bank's name, and makes sure they are only ever sent to their own floor, with their own limits on how many visitors they can bring. One partner bank's rush of customers can never spill onto another's floor, and nobody can wander into a bank they do not belong to.
s1_definition.oneliner: Identify the tenant on every request, stamp and propagate a verified tenant context, and enforce per-tenant routing, limits, quotas, and data isolation so tenants share the platform but never each other's data or capacity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Multi-tenancy is serving many independent customers, called tenants, from one shared platform while keeping each tenant's data, configuration, and resource usage strictly isolated. At the gateway, multi-tenancy is implemented by identifying the tenant on every request, from a subdomain, a path prefix, a header, or a claim in the JWT; attaching that tenant identity to the request context and propagating it downstream; and then applying per-tenant policy such as routing, rate limits, quotas, and data isolation. The gateway becomes the authoritative place where every request is stamped with a verified tenant so no tenant can ever see or affect another.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India runs a shared platform that several partner banks use, each a separate tenant. It is like one big office building where each partner bank rents its own floor. The security desk at the entrance, the gateway, looks at each visitor's pass to see which bank they belong to, stamps their file with that bank's name, and makes sure they are only ever sent to their own floor, with their own limits on how many visitors they can bring. One partner bank's rush of customers can never spill onto another's floor, and nobody can wander into a bank they do not belong to.

**One line to remember:** Identify the tenant on every request, stamp and propagate a verified tenant context, and enforce per-tenant routing, limits, quotas, and data isolation so tenants share the platform but never each other's data or capacity.

sections.s2_technical:
The first job is tenant identification, which must be reliable and must happen early at the gateway. Common strategies are a subdomain such as partnerbank.api.nbi.example.com, a path prefix such as the tenant ID at the start of the path, a header such as an X-Tenant-Id, or, most securely, a claim inside the authenticated JWT. The JWT claim is strongest because it is signed and cannot be forged, whereas a header alone can be spoofed, so a serious implementation derives the tenant from the token and treats any client-supplied header as untrusted unless it matches the token.

The second job is to put the resolved tenant into the request context and propagate it to every downstream service, usually as a trusted header the gateway injects after verification, like X-Tenant-Id. Downstream services read it to scope their data access. Because the gateway is the single point that stamps this, services can trust it, though in a zero-trust design they still validate it.

The third job is per-tenant routing. Different tenants may be served by different backends or different versions. The gateway can route tenant A to one service deployment and tenant B to another, which supports gradual rollouts per tenant or dedicated infrastructure for premium tenants. This is done with tenant-aware route predicates.

The fourth job is per-tenant traffic management: rate limits and quotas scoped to the tenant, so one tenant's traffic surge cannot starve another. This is the noisy-neighbor problem, and the gateway solves it by keying the rate limiter on the tenant, for example a token bucket per tenant ID in Redis. A premium tenant might get a higher limit than a basic one, which is also how you enforce commercial tiers.

The fifth job is data isolation, which the gateway enables but the data layer enforces. The common models are a separate database per tenant, a shared database with a separate schema per tenant, or a shared schema with a tenant-ID column on every row. The gateway's contribution is guaranteeing the tenant context is present and trustworthy, and often injecting it so the data layer can apply the right datasource or the right row filter. The strongest isolation is database-per-tenant; the most efficient is a shared schema with a discriminator column, and the choice is a trade-off between isolation and cost.

A senior nuance is per-tenant configuration and observability. Tenants often need different feature flags, different limits, and separately attributable logs and metrics, so the gateway tags every log and metric with the tenant ID, which lets you bill, debug, and alert per tenant. Another nuance is the security boundary: the most dangerous bug in a multi-tenant system is cross-tenant data leakage, so the tenant check must be mandatory and fail closed, meaning a request with no resolvable tenant is rejected, never defaulted to some tenant. A final nuance is that tenant resolution belongs at the edge precisely so that no downstream service has to re-derive it inconsistently.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers its core banking platform to several partner banks as tenants. Each partner's data must be completely isolated, and each has a commercial plan: a premium partner gets a high request rate, a basic partner a lower one. If one partner's app goes viral and floods the platform, it must not slow down the others. The gateway must identify the tenant, isolate its data, and enforce its own limit.

Problem 2 — A partner's client might try to spoof a tenant header to read another partner's data. The gateway must derive the tenant from the signed token, not from an untrusted header, so spoofing fails.

The connection to the fix: we will build a multi-tenant gateway that resolves the tenant from the token, rejects requests whose header disagrees with the token, enforces a per-tenant rate limit by plan, routes to a per-tenant datasource, and stamps the tenant onto the downstream call. The demo sends requests for two tenants, shows isolation, shows a spoof attempt failing, and shows one tenant's flood not affecting the other.

What the code will do. There is a `TenantRequest` with a token, an optional header tenant, and a path. There is a `TenantResolver` that extracts the tenant from the token and detects spoofing. There is a `TenantPlanRegistry` mapping tenant to plan and rate limit. There is a per-tenant `RateLimiter`. There is a `TenantDataRouter` that selects the tenant's datasource. There is a `MultiTenantGateway` chaining these. The demo runs premium and basic tenants, a spoof, and a basic-tenant flood.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the plain-Java multi-tenant demo
javac MultiTenantDemo.java
java com.bank.gateway.demo.MultiTenantDemo

# Real Spring Cloud Gateway: tenant resolved from JWT claim, X-Tenant-Id injected
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/multi-tenant-gateway-1.0.0.jar

# Call as a tenant (tenant derived from the token's tenant_id claim)
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <jwt-with-tenant_id=partner-premium>' \
  https://partner-premium.api.nbi.example.com/api/v1/accounts
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is requests for a premium tenant, a basic tenant, a spoof attempt, a basic flood, and a premium request during that flood.

Step 1. The premium request arrives. The resolver reads the tenant from the signed token as partner-premium. The header agrees, so there is no spoof. The plan registry returns the premium plan with a high rate limit. The per-tenant limiter allows it, and the data router selects the premium datasource. The gateway allows it and will propagate the premium tenant ID downstream.

Step 2. The basic request arrives. Its token resolves to partner-basic, the header agrees, and the basic plan is selected with its lower limit and its shared-schema datasource. It is allowed and routed to a completely different datasource than premium, which is the data isolation in action.

Step 3. The spoof request arrives with a token for partner-basic but a header claiming partner-premium. The resolver derives the true tenant from the token as basic, then detects that the header contradicts the token and rejects the request. Because the tenant comes from the signed token, the spoofed header cannot grant access to the premium tenant's data.

Step 4. The basic tenant floods with several requests. The per-tenant limiter counts only basic's requests against basic's low limit, so after a couple pass, the rest are rejected with 429. Crucially, this counter is keyed on the tenant.

Step 5. During that basic flood, a premium request arrives. Because the limiter is per-tenant, premium has its own separate budget that basic's flood never touched, so the premium request is allowed normally. This is the noisy-neighbor isolation working: one tenant's surge cannot starve another.

```
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] === Premium tenant request ===
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] ALLOW tenant=partner-premium plan=PREMIUM → datasource=premiumdb (propagate X-Tenant-Id downstream)
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] === Basic tenant request (different datasource) ===
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] ALLOW tenant=partner-basic plan=BASIC → datasource=shareddb[schema=basic] (propagate X-Tenant-Id downstream)
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] === Spoof attempt: header says premium, token says basic ===
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [SEVERE] REJECT: tenant spoof header=partner-premium token=partner-basic
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] === Basic tenant floods — its own limit trips, premium unaffected ===
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [WARNING] 429 rate limit for tenant=partner-basic (plan BASIC)
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [WARNING] 429 rate limit for tenant=partner-basic (plan BASIC)
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] === Premium still works during basic's flood ===
2026-10-24 14:10:01 [INFO] ALLOW tenant=partner-premium plan=PREMIUM → datasource=premiumdb (propagate X-Tenant-Id downstream)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Multi-tenancy is serving many independent customers, called tenants, from one shared platform while keeping each tenant's data, configuration, and resource usage completely isolated. The gateway is where I make this real, because it is the single place every request passes through, so it is the natural authority for identifying the tenant and stamping it onto the request. In my banking work at National Bank of India, we offered our core platform to several partner banks as tenants, each with its own data and its own commercial plan, and the gateway kept them cleanly separated.

The first and most important job is identifying the tenant reliably. I derive the tenant from a signed claim in the JWT, not from a client-supplied header, because a header can be spoofed while a signed token cannot. If a request arrives with a header claiming one tenant but a token belonging to another, the gateway rejects it as a spoof, which is exactly how we stop one partner from reaching another partner's data. Once resolved, the gateway attaches the tenant to the request context and propagates it downstream as a trusted header so the services can scope their data access to the right tenant.

After identification come the per-tenant policies. Routing can send different tenants to different backends, which supports dedicated infrastructure for premium partners or gradual per-tenant rollouts. Traffic management is keyed on the tenant, so each tenant has its own rate limit and quota by plan; this is how I solved the noisy-neighbor problem, because when one partner's app went viral and flooded the platform, the per-tenant limiter only counted that partner's traffic against that partner's budget, and the other partners kept running normally. Data isolation is the backbone: depending on the isolation and cost trade-off, I use a database per tenant for the strongest separation, a schema per tenant, or a shared schema with a tenant-ID column, and the gateway guarantees the tenant context is present and trustworthy so the data layer applies the correct datasource or row filter.

The nuances I always stress are the security boundary and observability. The worst possible bug in a multi-tenant system is cross-tenant data leakage, so the tenant check is mandatory and fails closed, meaning a request with no resolvable tenant is rejected outright and never quietly defaulted to some tenant. And because tenants need separate billing, debugging, and alerting, the gateway tags every log and metric with the tenant ID, so usage is attributable per tenant. Resolving the tenant at the edge is deliberate, because it means no downstream service has to re-derive it inconsistently, and the one place that stamps the identity is the one place I have to get right.
